### Abu Dhabi Enters Its Second Day With Prisoners on the Table, Asia Rises for a Third Day, and Oil Firms on a Struck Pipeline

Filed as: Edition No. 32 — The Overnight Watch · 2026-11-11T04:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-11-overnight-watch.html

The Night File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Abu Dhabi Enters Its Second Day With Prisoners on the Table, Asia Rises for a Third Day, and Oil Firms on a Struck Pipeline

 The night file, while Washington slept: Abu Dhabi's second day opened with the prisoner question as its only near thing and the land question still off the table; the war supplied its own overnight commentary in drones at both ends; Tehran denied the talks Washington describes; Asia bought the chips and sold the bonds; and the two Senate counts kept their dates and not their answers.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0400 ET, Wednesday, November 11, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 31, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today, which filed the House referral of the Hegseth articles, Tuesday's hot inflation print, Abu Dhabi's first day and Paris's close. The reports filed here are the night's reports, taken after that edition closed; where they restate Tuesday's facts, the restatement is identified. The midnight edition stands unrevised, as a log stands.

The Night in Brief

Abu Dhabi entered its second day with a prisoner exchange discussed and not agreed, the war ran underneath the talks in both directions overnight, Washington and Tehran contradicted each other on whether any negotiation exists, and Asia rose for a third day while the world's bonds fell. President Zelenskyy called Tuesday's first session constructive and quite substantive and Secretary Rubio called it very productive, in the Kyiv account and the productive account filed below; the prisoner question—1,000 a side in one account, 1,500 a side in another, agreed in the nearest time in a third and expressly not agreed in the president's own—is the file's central disagreement, printed whole in the Cocked Hat. No ceasefire and no agreement on land was announced, and the accounts agree the territorial question was not taken up on day one. In the night Russia launched 155 drones against Ukraine's energy system and Ukrainian drones reached the Baltic terminal at Ust-Luga, where the Leningrad governor counted 92 drones shot down; the Reuters sources put the share of Russian refining capacity disrupted since late October at about 30 percent. On Iran, Secretary Rubio said the blockade and sanctions make major combat unnecessary; Mr. Rezaei said no negotiations with the Americans are under way; and a tanker was struck near Hormuz on Tuesday while the Saudi pipeline attacked on Monday kept flowing. Asia's chip shares rose a third day and Brent firmed to about $92, against a global bond selloff on Tuesday's hot inflation print. In Jerusalem the Arab lists said they will vote for Mr. Kahana for speaker on November 17. Neither Senate race was called.

Abu Dhabi at 0400: Day Two, Prisoners Discussed, Land Not Taken Up

The second day is the fact the night adds to the Abu Dhabi file; everything else about the talks is a description, and the descriptions do not match. The delegations met for nearly four hours on Tuesday, the first three-way session since February, on humanitarian issues, possible prisoner exchanges and security guarantees, with no ceasefire and no political agreement, in the day's summary filed below. President Zelenskyy's account is the fullest from any principal: constructive and quite substantive; prisoner releases a priority; the nature of security guarantees discussed in detail; directives given to his team for Wednesday. Secretary Rubio's account is two words—very productive—with no details attached. A third account, in the morning briefing filed below, reports little concrete progress, citing Le Monde, and states that ceasefire and territorial issues were explicitly off the table on day one. Wednesday's session is the last of the scheduled two.

One American proposal entered the file overnight, and it enters as a single briefing's report. The Ukraine Monitor's morning briefing, filed below, reports a United States proposal to redraw the Donetsk and Luhansk oblast boundaries, letting Russia claim the full Donbas on paper while Ukraine retains the cities it holds, and calls it the most consequential diplomatic signal emerging from the process. No delegation's statement in the night file confirms the proposal, and President Zelenskyy's standing sentence is that Russia overstates how much of the Donbas it holds. The desk prints the report as a report, attributed to its source, and files no bearing beside it at 0400.

The War at 0400: 155 Drones One Way, 92 Counted the Other

The fighting supplied the night's hardest figures, and they run in both directions. Russia launched 155 drones against Ukraine on November 10, striking energy infrastructure in eight oblasts and hitting the Trypillia power plant, and a worker at the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant was lost to a drone strike, in the morning briefing filed below; power went out in part of Kryvyi Rih after a drone attack, in the Reuters account filed below. The same Reuters account carries the other direction's count: Russia shot down 92 drones early on Wednesday over the Leningrad region, Governor Drozdenko said, in an attack on the region that holds the ports of Ust-Luga, Primorsk and Vysotsk and the Kirishi refinery; the governor's account of the Ust-Luga strike, carried in the live file filed below, adds a fire and a power station cut off. The wider figure is the refiners': Ukrainian attacks since late October have disrupted about 30 percent of Russia's refining capacity, nine of its 35 major refineries in the past week alone, about 2.2 million barrels a day of capacity against a national total of roughly 6.8 million, on two industry sources in the Reuters account filed below. Monday's Kirishi strike, which set the plant on fire and killed a woman in the region, stands in both accounts. The talks and the strikes proceeded on the same hours; neither file mentions the other.

Washington and Tehran at 0400: No Need for Combat, No Talks at All

The Iran file gained two opposite sentences on Tuesday, and at 0400 they stand facing each other with nothing between them. Secretary Rubio, in Paris after the G7 meeting, said the president really does not have any need to conduct major combat operations against Iran, because the naval blockade and sanctions are doing the work—doing devastation to Iran's economy, in his words, and not a stalemate—in the Paris account and the diplomacy account filed below. Within hours Mr. Rezaei said Iran is not currently conducting any negotiations with the Americans. Foreign Minister Araghchi denied any plan for a meeting between Mr. Rezaei and Vice President Vance in Doha—entirely baseless, in his words—and wrote to the United Nations and the nuclear watchdog asking them to condemn an American cash reward for information on Iran's nuclear programme. The Qatari channel produced its own pair: Mr. Araghchi met the Qatari mediators, said the ideas would be carried to Washington, and hoped for a final response by Tuesday, in the mediators account filed below; an American official called those talks positive and constructive and set the condition that no agreement ends the war unless the nuclear programme is addressed. Tehran's two-day proposal stands where it stood: American steps first—blockade lifted, war ended on all fronts, funds released—and the strait reopened inside a week. The president has called the proposal unacceptable. No text, no meeting and no agreement exists in the file.

Hormuz at 0400: A Tanker Struck, a Pipeline Flowing, No Reopening

The strait's overnight file is an attack, a claim and a pipeline that did not stop. A tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile near Hormuz on Tuesday, with no injuries and no environmental impact reported, in the UKMTO report carried in the Asia account filed below; a second file reports hull damage to at least one vessel designated non-compliant in the southern channels on November 9, in the strait file filed below. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, struck Monday in the Medina region, kept flowing: a limited fire, extinguished, no injuries, operations unaffected, roughly four million barrels a day moving to Yanbu on the 1,200-kilometre line that is the kingdom's principal alternative to the strait, in the escalation check filed below. Yemen's Houthis claimed further strikes on several pumping stations on Tuesday; Saudi authorities have not confirmed them. Saudi Arabia also reported intercepting missiles and a drone on Tuesday. Responsibility for the Monday pipeline attack has not been conclusively established in any account in the file. No agreement on reopening the strait exists, and both blockades—Iran's of the strait, America's of Iran's ports—stand.

The Markets at 0400: Asia Rises a Third Day, the Bonds Fall Everywhere

Asia's Wednesday session split in two: the shares followed the chips up, and the bonds followed Tuesday's inflation print down. In the afternoon readings, the Nikkei rose about 1.2 percent to around 61,190, its third straight gain, and the KOSPI about 1.9 percent to near 5,340, with SK Hynix up about 5.5 percent and the KOSDAQ up about 4.6 percent, fast enough to trigger a buy-side sidecar, in the afternoon account filed below; the earlier Reuters print, filed below, has the regional index up 0.2 percent, the Nikkei up 0.6 percent and the KOSPI up 0.4 percent—the same session at an earlier hour, printed as such. SoftBank fell about 3 percent on a quarterly loss of about 1.1 trillion yen, $7 billion in the Reuters figure. Hong Kong and Shanghai fell. Brent firmed the other way from Tuesday: up 0.7 percent to $92.16 in the Reuters print, about 1 percent to around $92.50 in the afternoon accounts, after dropping as low as $89.16 overnight. The bond figures are single-valued in direction: the two-year Treasury yield surged 18 basis points overnight, Japan's 10-year rose 7 points to 2.755 percent and Australia's 6 points to 5.05 percent. Gold fell 2.6 percent overnight and recovered a fraction, to $4,030.56 in one print and about $4,050 in another.

The cause named in every market account is the same number the midnight edition closed with, and the argument now is about December's size and March's existence. Core prices rose 0.3 percent in October, a third straight month at that rate, against a 0.2 percent forecast; Governor Waller had said before the print that 0.3 percent would prompt him to consider a half-point increase on December 8–9. Futures now price the quarter-point as essentially locked in, with the half-point at 10 percent in the Reuters overnight print and near 15 percent in a Tuesday midmorning reading. Dallas Fed President Logan said policy stands about 50 points below the modestly restrictive level required, Chicago's President Goolsbee called the report borderline disturbing in one account, and Philadelphia's President Paulson backed gradual hikes. Goldman Sachs kept its December quarter-point call and added a third quarter-point hike in March 2027, taking its expected peak to 4.25–4.5 percent, with its first cut pushed to December 2027. Settled: an increase in December on every pricing in the file. Open: 25 or 50, and how many follow.

Jerusalem at 0400: The Arab Votes Put Mr. Kahana Ahead, and the Laws Move Before the Government

Jerusalem's night file converts Tuesday's swearing-in into a programme, and the programme runs ahead of the government it needs. The speaker vote set for November 17 acquired its arithmetic: representatives of the Arab lists confirmed Tuesday they will vote for Matan Kahana, effectively ensuring his election over Speaker Ohana, in the Le Monde account filed below. The numbers underneath stand as counted: Mr. Netanyahu's bloc 53, Mr. Eisenkot's coalition 48, the Arab parties 19, and 61 required. With the chair, Mr. Eisenkot's bloc intends to legislate before any government exists: a commission of inquiry into the October 7, 2023 failure, a rollback of laws on the judiciary, police and media, and a bill limiting a prime minister's terms, applicable to future elections. Behind the programme, the coalition negotiation continues on its known terms: one or two ultra-Orthodox lists are being courted, at the possible price of compromise on conscription reform, the issue Mr. Lieberman—named to chair the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee—has campaigned against compromising. Mr. Eisenkot's mandate runs to mid-December on the 28-day count, 42 days on the count with the extension the president may grant. Mr. Netanyahu remains prime minister. Settled: the house, the candidate, the date, and now the votes, on the Arab lists' own word. Open: the government.

Krak&oacute;w at 0400: The Suspect's Examination, and the Questions That Stay Open

Krak&oacute;w produced no new finding in the night, and the desk files the state of the examination exactly where Tuesday left it. The post-mortem examinations of all nine victims were completed on Monday; detailed forensic opinions may take weeks; an examination of the suspect's own body was expected separately on Tuesday, in the investigation account filed below. The prosecutors' position stands in its two parts: the evidence gathered points to the dead man as responsible for both the square shooting and the three deaths at the family home, and motive, ideological influence and possible assistance by others remain unresolved. Justice Minister &Zdot;urek's sentence from Tuesday—a very strong thread of right-wing extremism, on the computer traces and the silencer found in the car—stands beside the prosecutors' caution, unjoined by them. The city's mourning, set by the city through November 11, runs its last day today. Nothing in the night file moves any of those sentences.

The Count at 0400: Mississippi's Window Closed, Alaska Waits for Friday

For a ninth day neither Senate race was called, and the night changed neither margin; what changed is that Mississippi can now receive no more of the ballots it was waiting for. Tuesday was the last day for postmarked absentee ballots to arrive. The latest figures in the file are Tuesday afternoon's: Mr. Colom ahead of Senator Hyde-Smith by 2,607 votes out of 953,547 counted, in the Associated Press figures reported in the lead account filed below, and by about 2,700, at 99 percent counted, in the clarity account filed below; a third account's figure, 1,138, stands in the Cocked Hat as an earlier Wednesday-night posting carried in a file dated before the count it describes. Counties certify by Friday, November 13; the secretary of state declares final results by December 3; Mississippi has no automatic recount provision. In Alaska, Ms. Peltola's lead stands at 2,517 on the last posted count, 218,641 ballots, with roughly a quarter outstanding; the next count is set for November 13 and the ranked-choice tabulation for November 18, if no candidate passes 50 percent. Democrats hold at least 54 seats whatever the two races decide.

Wednesday Opens: A Last Day in Abu Dhabi, and a Week of Dates

The day the night hands over is a closing day in one capital and a counting week in the others. In Abu Dhabi the talks run their second and last scheduled day, with the prisoner exchange the only item any principal has called near. In Paris the G7 is finished and its Hormuz appeal stands unanswered. In Washington the House's referral stands and the December meeting is four weeks out, its size now the open question. In Jerusalem the Arrangements Committee work proceeds toward the November 17 speaker vote. In Mississippi the counties count toward Friday's certification with the ballot window shut; in Alaska the next batch posts Friday. In Krak&oacute;w the forensic work runs on its weeks-long clock. At Hormuz the tanker file and the pipeline file both stand open, and the strait stands closed in Tehran's word and blockaded in Washington's. The log proceeds to Wednesday.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On the prisoner exchange, discussed at more than a thousand in one account, at 1,000 or 1,500 a side in another, reportedly agreed in the nearest time in a third, and expressly not agreed in President Zelenskyy's own account—the widest triangle in the file, on the item nearest to agreement. On Abu Dhabi's first day, constructive and quite substantive in Kyiv's word, very productive in Washington's, and little concrete progress in a morning-paper reading. On Asia, the Nikkei up 0.6 percent in the early Reuters print and about 1.2 percent in the afternoon readings, the KOSPI up 0.4 and then about 1.9: one session, two hours of it. On Brent, $92.16 against about $92.50, after $89.16 overnight. On the December half-point, 10 percent in the overnight futures print against near 15 percent at Tuesday midmorning. On Mississippi, margins of 2,607 and about 2,700 from Tuesday afternoon against 1,138 in an account whose own dating places it before those counts. On whether talks with Iran exist at all, Washington's mediators called positive and constructive by an American official against Tehran's flat sentence that no negotiations are under way. Against the triangle, the night's single-valued facts are these: the talks entered a second day with nothing signed; 92 drones were counted down over the Leningrad region by its governor and 155 launched against Ukraine in the briefing count; about 30 percent of Russian refining capacity stands disrupted on the industry sources; a tanker was struck near Hormuz and the East-West pipeline kept flowing at about four million barrels a day; the Arab lists' votes put Mr. Kahana ahead for November 17; Mississippi's ballot window is closed; and no Senate race was called. The log proceeds to Wednesday.

 The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 24 items.

A second day of talks is expected on November 11.

The meeting produced no ceasefire and no political agreement. A second day is scheduled, and the central disagreements remain: Russia demands territorial and security concessions, and Ukraine refuses to surrender land or accept restrictions that could leave it open to another attack.

The file also records Secretary Rubio saying the United States has no need to restart major combat in Iran because sanctions are working.

 SubjectiveReuters, via 947 The Beast — Russia shoots down 92 drones over the Leningrad regionRussia shot down 92 drones early on Wednesday in an attack over the Leningrad region northwest of Moscow, Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said on Telegram. The region is home to the ports of Ust-Luga, Primorsk and Vysotsk, key for Russia's oil and grain exports on the Baltic Sea, as well as the Kirishi oil refinery, Russia's second-largest. Reuters could not immediately independently confirm the report. On Monday a drone struck the Kirishi refinery, setting the plant on fire and killing a woman in the region. In Ukraine, power went out in part of the central city of Kryvyi Rih after a drone attack, an official said on Telegram.

 SubjectiveThe Independent — the live file: Kyiv strikes Russia's northwestPresident Zelenskyy's comments came as his forces launched drones at Ust-Luga in Russia's northwest, regional governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said, adding that the strikes caused a fire and cut off a power station. Ukrainian drone attacks on oil refineries since October have reportedly cut Russia's refining capacity by 30 percent. In the past week alone, the strikes have disrupted operations and caused emergency situations at nine of the country's 35 major refineries, Reuters reported, citing unnamed sources.

 SubjectiveSeeking Alpha, carrying the Reuters account — Ukrainian drone strikes are said to disrupt 30 percent of Russia's oil refiningUkrainian drone attacks have disrupted approximately 30 percent of Russia's oil refining capacity since late October, intensifying fuel shortages and complicating Moscow's efforts to maintain diesel exports, Reuters reported Tuesday, citing two industry sources. The strikes have affected nine of Russia's 35 major refineries over the past week. Facilities targeted since late October have a combined processing capacity of about 2.2 million barrels per day, compared with Russia's total refining capacity of roughly 6.8 million barrels daily. Among the affected facilities are refineries in Ryazan, Yaroslavl and the Volga region. A Ukrainian drone strike Monday sparked a fire at the Kirishi refinery, Russia's second-largest, and killed one woman, according to regional officials.

Within hours, Mr. Rezaei said Iran is not currently conducting any negotiations with the Americans. Foreign Minister Araghchi denied any plan for a meeting between Mr. Rezaei and Vice President Vance in Doha, calling the reports entirely baseless, and asked the United Nations and the nuclear watchdog to condemn an American cash reward for information on Iran's nuclear programme. Mr. Araghchi's plan puts American moves on day one: an end to the blockade, an end to the war on all fronts and the release of frozen Iranian funds.

 SubjectiveChennai Online — Secretary Rubio says no need for an Iran attack as diplomacy advancesSecretary Rubio stated on Tuesday, November 11, 2026, that there was no need to attack Iran again, as diplomatic efforts to end the conflict were gaining momentum. Following the president's earlier comment about positive progress toward resolving the eight-month war, Mr. Rubio emphasized that the American economic campaign against Iran had been so effective that major military operations were unnecessary. He made the statement during the G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris. Tehran remains open to reopening Hormuz if Washington meets certain conditions, including ending the war, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ceasing port blockades. Foreign Minister Araghchi reiterated that military action or increased sanctions would not resolve the conflict, emphasizing the need for respectful diplomacy.

 SubjectiveAl Jazeera — Foreign Minister Araghchi meets Qatari mediators as the United States calls for nuclear talksForeign Minister Araghchi met with Qatari mediators in New York to discuss a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, while an American official said there would be no agreement to end the war unless Tehran's nuclear programme is addressed. Mr. Araghchi told Iranian media on Monday that the Qatari mediators would carry the ideas discussed at the meeting to the United States and that he hoped to receive Washington's final response by Tuesday. The Iranian plan calls on the United States to release frozen Iranian funds, lift sanctions and end its naval blockade of Iranian ports; those steps could be completed within four or five days, allowing the strait to reopen and negotiations on a final agreement, including on the nuclear programme, to begin by the seventh day. The president rejected the proposal on Saturday, calling it unacceptable. The talks were positive and constructive, the official said, but stressed there would be no agreement unless Iran's nuclear programme is addressed. Rear Admiral Sayyari insisted that the Strait of Hormuz remains closed.

 SubjectiveSchaaf Media — the Middle East escalation check, November 10Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline was struck in the Medina region on November 9. According to the Energy Ministry, the attack caused a limited fire that was subsequently extinguished; no injuries or fatalities were reported, and pipeline operations remained unaffected. The approximately 1,200-kilometre route currently transports around four million barrels per day to Yanbu, and it is Saudi Arabia's principal alternative to the restricted Hormuz route. Responsibility for the attack has not been conclusively established. On November 10 Saudi Arabia reported intercepting additional missiles and a drone over the Eastern Province, and two missiles targeting Riyadh and another in the south. No agreement on the safe reopening of Hormuz has been reached, and the United States blockade of Iranian ports remains in place.

 SubjectiveRegion Alert — Hormuz Strait intelligence: traffic, oil and harassmentThe assessment rates the threat index at high as of November 10. The Saudi East-West pipeline sustained a strike on November 9 in the Medina sector, causing an exterior facility fire that emergency teams extinguished within two hours without halting crude flow; the 1,200-kilometre line continues pumping roughly 4.0 million barrels per day to Yanbu. Brent crude front-month futures traded at $91.88 per barrel on November 10, down from $97.00 on November 9 and $118.00 on October 30, in this file's table.

 SubjectiveAsia Today — Asian markets extend the tech-led rebound despite hot United States inflationAsian stock markets extended their technology-led rebound on Wednesday, with Japan's Nikkei 225 rising about 1.2 percent to around 61,190 for a third consecutive session and South Korea's KOSPI climbing about 1.9 percent to near 5,340, even as hotter-than-expected United States inflation hardened expectations of further Federal Reserve increases. All index levels in this article are afternoon readings, taken while the Tokyo and Seoul markets were still trading.

 SubjectiveReuters — bonds reel as hot inflation fuels jumbo Fed hike fearsGlobal bonds tumbled and the dollar stayed firm after a hot United States inflation print and hawkish central bank rhetoric raised the risk of an outsized half-point rate hike from the Federal Reserve next month, though stocks remained resilient. Core inflation ran at a monthly rate of 0.3 percent in October, higher than the forecast 0.2 percent. Before the data landed, Governor Waller said a core reading of 0.3 percent would prompt him to consider a 50-basis-point hike in December. Dallas Fed President Logan said two more rate rises were needed, possibly rapidly; Chicago Fed President Goolsbee warned of a real inflation issue; Philadelphia Fed President Paulson called for gradual hikes. Fed funds futures imply a quarter-point move is essentially locked in, with a 10 percent probability of a 50-point rise, and three quarter-point moves fully priced by the middle of next year. Two-year Treasury yields surged 18 basis points overnight; Japan's 10-year yield rose 7 points to 2.755 percent and Australia's 6 points to 5.05 percent. In Asia, the broadest MSCI index rose 0.2 percent, the Nikkei climbed 0.6 percent and the KOSPI rose 0.4 percent, while China's blue chips lost 0.2 percent. SoftBank slid 3.3 percent after a $7 billion second-quarter net loss. Brent rose 0.7 percent to $92.16, having dropped as low as $89.16 overnight; gold fell 2.6 percent overnight before edging up 0.2 percent to $4,030.56.

 SubjectiveReuters — investors boost the odds of a half-point Fed hike as the core rise meets Governor Waller's barOdds the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates half a percentage point at its December meeting jumped on Tuesday after new data showed prices rising faster than expected and clearing the bar set by one key policymaker for considering a quicker pace. The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent month over month in October, down from 0.6 percent in September as energy inflation receded, but the core index rose 0.3 percent for the third month in a row. In comments overnight in London, Governor Waller said a core reading of 0.3 percent for October would prompt him to consider a half-point hike at the December 8–9 meeting. Market bets on a larger increase were rapidly building amid a broad bond selloff and at midmorning were close to 15 percent. The data and the comments drove a selloff in the Treasury market, with the two-year yield rising by the most since early April 2025.

 SubjectiveReuters — the bond storm of 2026 may be passing, but Fed gusts lingerThe great sovereign bond storm of 2026 may be clearing, as an apparent truce in the United States–Iran war offers investors their first glimpse of calm after months of oil-fuelled turmoil. Brent rocketed more than 70 percent to a four-year high of $120 a barrel in April, before falling below $90 this week. Data on Tuesday showed inflation remains high and is running at almost twice the Fed's target. Before Tuesday's hot consumer price report, Governor Waller suggested the central bank may need to get even tougher: a core rise of 0.3 percent would prompt him to consider a half-point hike in December, twice the usual increment. Dallas Fed President Logan said later that policy was still about 50 basis points below the modestly restrictive level required. At annual headline rates almost twice the target, real policy rates are still close to zero even though unemployment is only 4.1 percent, the economy is likely growing at more than 3 percent, and financial conditions are still historically loose, in the column's figures.

 SubjectiveLe Monde — Mr. Eisenkot pledges swift legislative reforms before government formation in IsraelThe inauguration day for the new Knesset on Tuesday, November 10, unfolded much like the election campaign: chaotic, loud and tense. The four parties making up the opposition coalition agreed on a candidate for speaker: Matan Kahana, 54, an MP from Mr. Eisenkot's party, expected to be elected in a vote scheduled for November 17. Kahana served as minister of religious affairs between 2021 and 2022 and is a former fighter pilot and reserve colonel; he is set to succeed Amir Ohana, who has held the post for four years. Mr. Netanyahu's bloc has secured 53 seats, ahead of Mr. Eisenkot's coalition with 48, but representatives of the Arab lists confirmed on Tuesday they would vote for Kahana, effectively ensuring his victory. Although no government has been formed, the Knesset can already pass legislation, and Mr. Eisenkot and his allies aim to move quickly: the first major law could create a commission of inquiry into the October 7, 2023 security failure, and the coalition also intends to begin rolling back laws affecting the judiciary, police and media, and to discuss a bill limiting a prime minister's terms. Negotiations are under way to persuade one or two ultra-Orthodox lists to join the majority, even if it means partially compromising on the promise to reform conscription. Mr. Eisenkot has up to 42 days from his appointment on Sunday to form a majority.

 SubjectiveThe Media Line, via SRN News — Israel's 26th Knesset sworn in as the opposition calls for a new speakerIsrael's 26th Knesset was sworn in Tuesday in Jerusalem, as opposition lawmakers launched an effort to replace Speaker Amir Ohana and Prime Minister Netanyahu called for a national unity government to confront continuing threats from Iran. All 120 lawmakers took the oath of office, in a ceremony marked by political confrontations and appeals for unity. The Yashar party, led by Mr. Eisenkot, announced that 67 lawmakers had signed a formal request to remove Mr. Ohana and nominate former minister Matan Kahana as his replacement. The Change Bloc had earlier secured the 61 signatures needed to initiate the process, with a vote expected next week.

 SubjectiveMK Niralo — the Kraków suspect dies in hospital as the terrorism investigation continuesThe 24-year-old suspected of carrying out the November 7 mass shooting in Kraków died in hospital at about 4:30 a.m. on Monday, November 9, after three operations, having been shot by police on Saturday. Prosecutors are treating the public attack—six people killed in the square, and three relatives found dead at his home—as a suspected terrorist offence, while stressing that motive, ideological influence and possible assistance by others remain unresolved. Post-mortem examinations of all nine victims were completed on Monday; detailed forensic opinions may take weeks. An examination of the suspect's body was expected separately on Tuesday. The National Prosecutor's Office said evidence gathered so far points to the man as the person responsible for both the public shooting and the three deaths at the family home.

 SubjectiveCNBC figures, via Suara Garut — Mr. Colom maintains a narrow lead in the Mississippi Senate raceDemocratic candidate Scott Colom maintained a narrow advantage over incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith, in a contest that could end a Republican winning streak dating back to 1982 and give Mississippi its first Democratic senator in nearly four decades. According to Associated Press figures reported by CNBC, Mr. Colom led Ms. Hyde-Smith by 2,607 votes out of 953,547 ballots counted as of 4:30 p.m. ET on November 10. Mississippi's certification deadline is November 13, while the secretary of state must declare the final results by December 3. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan by 2,517 votes, with 218,641 ballots counted and an estimated 76 percent of the vote reported in the earlier update. Alaska requires more than 50 percent to win outright; if neither leading candidate reaches that threshold, ranked-choice voting will redistribute second preferences. The remaining ballot count is scheduled to be completed by November 18, with November 25 set as the state's target date for confirming results.

 SubjectiveUSA Today — why clarity in the Mississippi Senate election could come by week's endMississippi Democratic challenger Scott Colom was narrowly leading incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith as of 2:55 p.m. ET on November 10, with a margin of about 2,700 votes in a race with almost 1 million votes, or 99 percent of the total vote counted, according to results from USA Today. The Mississippi and Alaska Senate races have been too close to call since Election Day on November 3, as ballots continued arriving. Secretary of State Watson said in a November 4 statement that about 3,600 mail-in ballots, legally permitted to arrive and be counted up until November 10 if postmarked by Election Day, were still outstanding. November 13 is another key deadline: all 82 counties must certify their results by that day. In Alaska, as of 3 p.m. ET on November 10, Ms. Peltola was leading Senator Sullivan by a little more than 2,500 voters, with about 78 percent of the votes counted. If no candidate gets more than 50 percent, the ranked-choice tally would not start until November 18.

 SubjectiveAl Jazeera — what is delaying the Senate election results in Mississippi and AlaskaAs of Wednesday night, two Senate races remain undecided, and the Democrats will usher in the 120th Congress on January 3 with a majority of at least 54 seats. In Mississippi, both candidates hold about 49 percent, according to the Associated Press, with 96 percent of ballots counted so far; Mr. Colom was leading Ms. Hyde-Smith by 1,138 votes in this account's Wednesday-night figure, with a few thousand provisional and mail-in absentee ballots left to be counted. Secretary of State Watson counted roughly 3,600 mail-in ballots still to be tallied, along with an unknown number of affidavit ballots; counties have ten days from the election to submit certified results, which is November 13. In Alaska, Ms. Peltola leads Senator Sullivan by 637 votes in this account's figure, with nearly a quarter of the votes uncounted; ranked-choice results will not be published until November 18, fifteen days after the election. A second candidate named Daniel Sullivan appears on the ballot.

### The House Refers the Hegseth Articles to Committee, 211 to 204, and Abu Dhabi Ends Its First Day Without an Agreement

Filed as: Edition No. 31 — The Midnight Watch · 2026-11-11T00:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-11-midnight-watch.html

The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 The House Refers the Hegseth Articles to Committee, 211 to 204, and Abu Dhabi Ends Its First Day Without an Agreement

 The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: the impeachment effort ended in a committee referral, 211 to 204, on the same day its target conceded nothing at the Pentagon; the inflation number came in hot and closed; Abu Dhabi’s first day produced an agenda, a duration and no agreement; Paris closed without a statement; and both Senate counts kept their secrets for another night.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Wednesday, November 11, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 30, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Tuesday, and in Tuesday’s earlier editions, Nos. 29 and 28. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Tuesday Settled, What It Left Open

Tuesday settled its vote, its number and its two swearing-in facts, and it left both of its wars, both of its counts and the size of its December increase open, and the desk files the day in that order. The House voted 211 to 204 in the evening to refer Representative Massie’s eight articles against Secretary Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, a referral that ends the impeachment effort in this Congress; the secretary had conceded nothing at the Pentagon in the morning, and he does not have to. The Bureau of Labor Statistics put October consumer prices up 0.4 percent and core prices up 0.3 percent for a third straight month, a tenth above the consensus on both measures, meeting the test Governor Waller set that morning for considering a half-point increase in December; Wall Street closed lower, on figures the closing accounts do not state identically, and Brent settled at $91.49 after trading below ninety dollars for the first time since August. In Abu Dhabi the first day of the three-way talks ended after about four hours with no agreement announced, the subjects named—security guarantees, humanitarian questions, prisoner exchanges—and the question of land carried to Wednesday. In Paris the G7 foreign ministers finished their two days with Secretary Rubio saying Europe is at the table and reporting, in his own words, no response to his appeal that other nations step up in the Strait of Hormuz. In Jerusalem the 26th Knesset was sworn in, the bloc behind Mr. Eisenkot named Matan Kahana for speaker, and Speaker Ohana set the vote on his replacement for November 17. In Krak&oacute;w the justice minister named a strong thread of right-wing extremism in the gunman’s computer; the prosecutors have established no ideology. Neither Senate race was called: Mississippi’s ballot window closed with Mr. Colom ahead by about 2,700 votes, and Alaska’s Tuesday batch had not posted, leaving Ms. Peltola ahead by 2,517 on Monday’s count.

Washington at Midnight: 211 to 204, and the Articles Go to Committee

The evening supplied the result the day had scheduled and the 1800 file did not hold. The House voted 211 to 204 to refer the eight articles to the Judiciary Committee, in the Al Jazeera account and The Times account filed below. The referral disposes of the resolution without testing it: impeachment requires 218 votes on the articles themselves, and no vote on the articles was taken. Mr. Massie, who filed the articles, was the only Republican to vote against the referral—the only member of his party who voted to keep his own resolution alive.

What follows is procedure, and the procedure is the settlement. The committee is controlled by the president’s allies, who set its schedule; the expectation in the accounts filed below is that the matter will not be taken up before this Congress ends on January 3, when the articles formally expire. The Journal’s account adds the other side’s stated intention: House Democrats are expected to revive the effort when they take control in January, which would require new articles. The articles remain allegations in a charging document, found by no court, now filed in a committee. Settled: the vote and the margin. Open: January.

The Number at Midnight: Hot, Closed, and Carried to December

The day’s one scheduled number is a closed fact, and midnight repeats it once, exactly. Consumer prices rose 0.4 percent in October after 0.6 percent in September; core prices rose 0.3 percent, as in September and in August. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 0.3 and 0.2. No annual rate exists, because the bureau collected no October 2025 data during last year’s lapse in appropriations. The next report, covering November, is scheduled for December 10—one day after the meeting this report feeds.

The response the number met was written before it landed. Governor Waller, in London remarks published that morning, said he was leaning toward a 25-basis-point increase at the December 8–9 meeting even if October improved, and that if core prices rose around 0.3 percent or higher, a 50-basis-point increase should be considered. Core printed 0.3 percent. The governor’s condition is met on his own stated terms; the committee’s decision has not been taken, and it is not his alone. The pricing accounts agree on the direction and differ on the figure, as they have all day: an increase of at least 25 basis points fully priced in the wire account filed below, up from 84 percent on Monday; the odds of the half-point move at 15.3 percent after the print in the FedWatch figures filed below, and near 10 percent in a late-afternoon reading in another account. Settled: the print, and that December brings an increase on every pricing in the file. Open: its size.

The Close at Midnight: Lower on Every Account, the Figures Apart

Wall Street closed lower, and that is the whole of what the closing accounts agree on to the last figure. The desk’s evening table, carried at 1800, put the S&P 500 down 0.38 percent at 7,520.93, the Nasdaq Composite down 0.74 percent at 25,065.88, the Dow down 0.30 percent at 52,231.89, and Nvidia down 5.47 percent at $168.89, in the closing account filed below. The Reuters closing account filed below puts the same three indexes lower still: the Dow down 0.43 percent at 52,166.63, the S&P 500 down 0.64 percent at 7,501.88, and the Nasdaq down 1.15 percent at 24,962.44. The two tables cannot both be the close, and the desk does not choose between them at midnight; both stand in the Cocked Hat, and the evening edition stands unrevised. What no account disputes: the two-year Treasury yield rose 19.1 basis points to 4.738 percent, its largest daily gain since April 2025 in the Reuters account; Anthropic’s filing of a $70 to $78 price range for its offering, in the TechCrunch account filed below, steadied the technology shares at mid-morning without saving the close; and Brent settled at $91.49 after trading below ninety dollars for the first time since August, in the oil account filed below.

Abu Dhabi at Midnight: Four Hours, the Subjects Named, and the Land Carried to Wednesday

The first three-way meeting since February is a fact; everything beyond its duration and its agenda is a claim, and the desk files them separately. The session ran nearly four hours in the wire account filed below, and four and a half hours including a break in a second account the evening edition carried. The subjects, across the accounts filed below, were security guarantees, humanitarian questions and possible prisoner exchanges, in the day’s summary filed below; Mr. Kushner argued at the opening for a new security architecture for Europe, in the opening account filed below. No agreement, no ceasefire and no joint statement was announced. The talks resume on Wednesday, and the question the first day did not settle is the oldest one in the file: Russia demands territorial and security concessions, Ukraine refuses to surrender land, and Foreign Minister Lavrov said Russia would not agree to an immediate ceasefire without knowing what would happen next, in the Reuters account filed below.

One account calls the day a collapse and attributes to President Zelenskyy a rejection of any Donbas exchange, in the partisan account filed below; no delegation’s statement confirms it. The fighting did not pause for the opening: Russian forces struck 10 regions overnight, hit five major substations, and killed two people in Vinnytsia, in the Reuters account above; the drone count runs from 162 in one Ukrainian count to more than 300 in another. In Paris, Mr. Sybiha urged Secretary Rubio to accelerate interceptor deliveries, in the Reuters interview filed below.

Paris at Midnight: Two Days End, and an Appeal Answered With Silence

The G7 foreign ministers finished their two days in Paris on Tuesday, and the meeting closed without a joint statement in the file at midnight. On Ukraine, Secretary Rubio said Europe is at the table and the trilateral format should eventually include the European partners, in the Paris account filed below; Foreign Minister Wadephul answered that any security architecture must involve Europe directly. On Hormuz, the secretary pressed the other nations to step up on shipping and acknowledged making no headway: “I raised it. I didn’t get a response,” in the Associated Press account filed below. Settled: the meeting is over, and Europe’s seat remains a subject of negotiation rather than a seat. Open: who, if anyone, joins the American ships.

Jerusalem at Midnight: Sworn In, a Candidate Named, and a Vote Set for November 17

The 26th Knesset exists; that much Tuesday settled in full. Its members were sworn in at Jerusalem, Speaker Ohana took the chair for the opening, and the arithmetic of the house stands as the final count published it: the prime minister’s bloc holds 53 of 120 seats, the parties against him 48, and the Arab parties 19, and a government needs 61, in the swearing-in account filed below. Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc announced its agreed candidates for the period of forming a government—Matan Kahana of Yashar for speaker, and Mr. Liberman to chair the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee—in the agreement account filed below.

The vote that tests those numbers now has a date and an hour. Speaker Ohana, who received the request signed by 67 lawmakers, said he had scheduled the vote on his replacement for Tuesday, November 17, at 4 p.m., in the swearing-in account above. United Torah Judaism has said it will not vote to replace the speaker before a government is formed, so the count on the 17th will show whether 61 votes exist without the Haredi parties—the first hard number of the new house. Mr. Eisenkot’s mandate runs 28 days from November 8, with a possible 14-day extension. Settled: the house is sworn, the candidate is named, the vote is dated. Open: the government, which does not yet exist.

Krak&oacute;w at Midnight: A Minister Names an Ideology, the Prosecutors Have Not

Krak&oacute;w’s file gained a minister’s conclusion on Tuesday and kept the prosecutors’ caution beside it, and midnight is the hour to print the two side by side without joining them. Justice Minister &Zdot;urek, in a radio interview, said investigators had found a silencer in the gunman’s car and, on his computer, traces of visits to websites devoted to Anders Breivik, and that there is a very strong thread of right-wing extremism, in the minister’s account and the second account filed below. He put the ammunition found at nearly 500 rounds, with numerous firearms magazines. The gunman left no note and no manifesto, in the same accounts.

Against the minister’s sentence stands the record of the office conducting the case. On Monday the prosecutors said it was too early to identify an ideological motivation; they treat the attack as a suspected terrorist offence while stating that motive, influence and assistance remain unresolved, in the investigation account filed below. The examinations of all nine victims were completed on Monday; detailed forensic opinions may take weeks. Thirteen of the injured remained in hospital in the evening file. Settled: what was found, as the minister states it. Open: what the prosecutors will establish.

Iran at Midnight: The Demands Restated, the Blockade Standing

The Iran file produced no new movement on Tuesday, and the desk files the restatement as the day’s fact. Foreign Minister Araghchi said the conflict will not be resolved through military means or by intensifying sanctions, and that the only solution is diplomacy addressing Iran’s demands, which were outlined in the two-day proposal and remain on the table, in the Tehran account filed below. The demands, as the accounts in the file list them, are an end to the war on all fronts, the release of frozen funds, the lifting of oil sanctions and an end to the American counter-blockade of Iranian ports; Tehran proposes to reopen Hormuz within two days in return. Washington’s position stands where Monday left it: the war effectively over in the president’s words, renewed strikes quite unlikely, and the naval blockade and Operation Iron Gate kept in place, in the account filed below. Secretary Rubio’s sentence also stands: negotiators are not on the verge of a breakthrough. The market went on translating the standoff into a price: Brent traded below ninety dollars and settled at $91.49. No agreement, no text and no new sentence from either capital toward one exists in the file at midnight.

The Count at Midnight: Mississippi’s Window Closed, Alaska’s Batch Still to Come

For an eighth day neither Senate race was called, and Tuesday changed both files by calendar rather than by count. In Mississippi, Tuesday was the last day for absentee ballots postmarked by Election Day to arrive and for affidavit voters to cure their identification. The afternoon tally put Mr. Colom ahead of Senator Hyde-Smith by about 2,700 votes, at 49.1 percent to 48.8 percent with 99 percent counted in that tally, in the clarity account filed below; the wire estimate this paper has carried stands at about 97 percent counted and a margin of 2,574 in its last raw posting, and the two completeness figures stand unreconciled in the Cocked Hat. Counties certify by Friday, November 13. Mississippi has no automatic recount provision, and the account filed below expects clarity by the week’s end.

In Alaska, Monday’s count stands as the last posted count: Ms. Peltola 106,321 first-choice votes, 48.63 percent, to Senator Sullivan’s 103,804, 47.48 percent—a margin of 2,517, up from 637—in the count account and the Juneau account filed below. The large Tuesday batch had not posted at midnight. A second candidate named Daniel Sullivan holds 3,651 votes, more than the margin, and the president has declared the race over while about a quarter of the vote remains outstanding, in the declaration account filed below; the count itself has declared nothing. The next updates are scheduled for November 13 and November 18, when the ranked-choice tabulation is set to run. Settled: Mississippi can receive no more ballots. Open: both seats, and whether the incoming majority stands at 54, 55 or 56.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On the close, the desk’s evening table against the Reuters closing account: the S&P 500 down 0.38 percent at 7,520.93 in the one, down 0.64 percent at 7,501.88 in the other; the Nasdaq down 0.74 against down 1.15; the Dow down 0.30 against down 0.43—one direction, three different landfalls, and the desk does not paper over the difference. On Abu Dhabi’s duration, nearly four hours in the wire account against four and a half including a break in a second. On Abu Dhabi’s character, a productive first day in the secretary’s word and an adjournment without agreement in the record, against a collapse in one partisan account that no delegation’s statement confirms. On the overnight attack, 162 drones and a ballistic missile in one Ukrainian count against more than 300 drones in another. On the December half-point, odds of 15.3 percent after the print in one instrument against about 10 percent in a late-afternoon reading in another, with the quarter-point fully priced in both. On Anthropic, $1.404 trillion fully diluted against about $968 billion at the midpoint on the post-offering count in the evening file: a difference of definition. On Mississippi’s completeness, 99 percent in the afternoon tally against about 97 percent in the wire estimate. On Alaska’s remainder, about 76 percent counted in the wire estimate against about 78 percent in another account and 26 percent outstanding in a third. Against the triangle, the day’s single-valued facts are these: the House referred the articles, 211 to 204, with one Republican against the referral; prices rose 0.4 percent and core prices 0.3 percent, a tenth hot on both measures, and Governor Waller’s stated condition was met by the core print; the 26th Knesset was sworn in and its speaker vote set for November 17; Abu Dhabi’s first day ended without an announced agreement and resumes Wednesday; Mississippi’s ballot window is closed; and no Senate race was called. Wednesday holds the second day in Abu Dhabi and the Alaska batch. The log turns.

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 29 items.

 SubjectiveAssociated Press, via Military.com — Secretary Rubio urges nations to step up on Strait of Hormuz securitySecretary Rubio pressed other nations on Tuesday to step up and help protect shipping from Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, and acknowledged making no headway on the issue with his G7 counterparts during two days of talks in Paris. “I raised it. I didn’t get a response,” he said. The United States will continue to defend shipping through the waterway, where vessels continue to face drone attacks.

 SubjectiveDevDiscourse — “Europe’s at the table”: Secretary Rubio reaffirms transatlantic unity on UkraineSpeaking at the G7 foreign ministers’ meeting in Paris, Secretary Rubio dismissed concerns of a rift over the Ukraine negotiations: Europe is at the table, the goals are the same, and the trilateral format should eventually include the European partners, because they are part of solving the problem for the long term. German Foreign Minister Wadephul stressed that any post-conflict security architecture must involve Europe directly.

 SubjectiveReuters — Ukraine urges the United States to speed up interceptor deliveries as Russia targets the power gridUkraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said he had urged Secretary Rubio on Tuesday to accelerate interceptor deliveries as Russia ramps up attacks on energy infrastructure as winter approaches. Ukraine remained prepared to discuss de-escalatory measures, including ceasefires covering the Black Sea and energy infrastructure, and proposals for a Black Sea ceasefire had been conveyed to Russia through intermediaries including Turkey, Egypt and India.

 SubjectiveSilent Dossier — the Knesset sworn in: can the prime minister stop the coalition?Israel’s 26th Knesset was sworn in at Jerusalem on Tuesday. The final count gave the prime minister’s bloc 53 of 120 seats, the anti-Netanyahu parties 48 and the Arab parties 19; a government needs 61. Speaker Ohana said he had scheduled the vote on his replacement for Tuesday, November 17, at 4 p.m., after 67 lawmakers signed a request to remove him. Mr. Eisenkot has 28 days from November 8 to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension.

 SubjectiveIndia This Week, carrying ANI — the Eisenkot-led bloc agrees on Matan Kahana for Knesset speakerMr. Eisenkot announced on Tuesday an agreement with his partners—Mr. Bennett, Mr. Golan, Mr. Liberman and Mr. Lapid—on candidates for key positions in the 26th Knesset during the period of forming a government: former minister Matan Kahana for speaker, and former Defense Minister Liberman to head the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee. Mr. Eisenkot received the mandate after 67 lawmakers recommended him, against 46 for the prime minister.

 SubjectiveEuropean Interest — Justice Minister &Zdot;urek reveals facts about the Krak&oacute;w shooter’s extremist identityInvestigators found a silencer in the gunman’s car and, on his computer, traces of visits to websites devoted to Anders Breivik. Justice Minister &Zdot;urek said there is a very strong thread of right-wing extremism. Investigators also found numerous firearms magazines and nearly 500 rounds of ammunition. The autopsy examinations are to determine whether the ammunition was military-grade or specialised semi-jacketed ammunition, which inflicts greater damage.

 SubjectiveTownhall — an official says the Krak&oacute;w shooter was a right-wing extremist after prosecutors urged cautionThe day after prosecutors said it was too early to identify an ideological motivation, Justice Minister &Zdot;urek told a radio station on Tuesday that evidence points strongly toward a right-wing motivation: the gunman visited websites concerning Anders Breivik, and other symbols at his workplace could point the same way. The gunman left no suicide note and no manifesto. Investigators are still determining whether he acted alone or had connections to extremist groups.

 SubjectiveMK Niralo — the Krak&oacute;w suspect dies in hospital as the terrorism investigation continuesThe 24-year-old suspect died in hospital at about 4:30 a.m. on Monday, November 9, after three operations, having been shot by police on Saturday. Prosecutors are treating the public attack—six people killed in the square, and three relatives found dead at his home—as a suspected terrorist offence, while stressing that the motive, any ideological influence and possible assistance by others remain unresolved. Examinations of all nine victims were completed on Monday; detailed forensic opinions may take weeks.

 SubjectiveThe Nigerian News — Iran urges the United States to meet its demands to end the warForeign Minister Araghchi said on Tuesday that the conflict will not be resolved through military means or by intensifying sanctions, and that the only solution is diplomacy that addresses Iran’s demands, which were outlined in the two-day proposal and remain on the table. The conditions include ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the American counter-blockade of Iranian ports. Tehran proposes to reopen Hormuz within two days in return.

 SubjectiveAnewZ — the president pauses Iran strikes and keeps the Hormuz blockadePresident Trump said on Monday he would hold off on new military strikes against Iran for now, after appeals from the Gulf countries, but would keep the naval blockade in place. He named Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the Emirates, Bahrain and Kuwait among those wanting Washington to avoid new attacks. Tehran gave the meeting a cool reception: Mr. Rezaei said Washington should stop manufacturing fake news about imaginary talks and surrender to the seven conditions.

 SubjectiveUSA Today — why clarity in the Mississippi Senate election could come by week’s endMr. Colom was narrowly leading Senator Hyde-Smith as of 2:55 p.m. ET on Tuesday, by about 2,700 votes in a race with almost one million votes cast, or 99 percent of the total counted in this tally. Tuesday was the last day for absentee ballots to arrive. Counties certify by Friday, November 13, and Mississippi has no automatic recount. In Alaska, Ms. Peltola led Senator Sullivan by a little more than 2,500 votes with about 78 percent counted in this account.

 SubjectiveCongress Countdown — the Alaska Senate race: why it is not called and when the count will moveThe race is not called. Ms. Peltola led Senator Sullivan by 2,517 votes in the November 10 count—106,321 votes, 48.63 percent, to 103,804, 47.48 percent—with about 76 percent of the expected vote counted in the Associated Press estimate carried here. A second candidate named Daniel Sullivan holds 3,651 votes, more than the margin. Further updates are scheduled for November 13 and November 18, when the last overseas ballots are due and the ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled if no candidate passes 50 percent.

 SubjectiveJuneau Empire — Ms. Peltola extends her lead over Senator Sullivan as ballot-counting continuesMs. Peltola extended her lead in the updated total published Monday: 2,517 first-choice votes, up from 637, after the Division of Elections added about 4,900 ballots. A larger batch—tens of thousands of absentee and early ballots—was expected on Tuesday. If she remains short of an outright majority of first choices on November 18, the ranked-choice tabulation decides the seat. Ballot Measure 2, seeking to repeal the open-primary and ranked-choice system, continues to trail, with 52.3 percent voting no.

 SubjectiveIndependent Voter News — the president declares the Alaska Senate race over; it is notThe president claimed the Alaska Senate race was over, while about 26 percent of the statewide vote remained outstanding—60,000 to 75,000 votes in this account—and Ms. Peltola led. A batch released on Monday expanded her lead from under 700 votes to a little over 2,500, at 48.63 percent to 47.48 percent. The results may not be known until next week.

 SubjectiveTechCrunch — Anthropic sets an IPO price range of $70 to $78 a shareAnthropic set a price range of $70 to $78 a share for its initial public offering, reaching an implied valuation of $1.404 trillion on the fully diluted count carried in this account. The filing steadied the technology shares at mid-morning on Tuesday after the hot inflation print had opened them lower.

 SubjectiveRigzone, carrying Bloomberg — oil prices retreat as peace hopes growOil prices retreated on Tuesday as hopes of a diplomatic resolution in the Middle East grew. Brent traded below ninety dollars a barrel for the first time since August during the session and settled at $91.49 in the closing figures the evening edition carried.
