### The House Takes Up the Hegseth Articles With No Vote in the File, Wall Street Closes Lower on the Hot Print, and Abu Dhabi Ends Its First Day Without an Agreement

Filed as: Edition No. 30 — The Evening Watch · 2026-11-10T18:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-10-evening-watch.html

The Evening File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 The House Takes Up the Hegseth Articles With No Vote in the File, Wall Street Closes Lower on the Hot Print, and Abu Dhabi Ends Its First Day Without an Agreement

 The evening file: the day’s developments whole, and the first considered responses from every side. The day gave one number, one witness, one close, and two tables. The number was hot, the witness conceded nothing, the close was lower, and neither table produced an agreement.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1800 ET, Tuesday, November 10, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 29, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 today, and from Edition No. 28, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today. Where the evening figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open, and the earlier editions stand unrevised, as a log stands.

The Evening in Brief

The day settled its number and its market, opened its two negotiations without closing either, named its speaker candidate and set that vote a week out, and left its two Senate counts and its one impeachment vote exactly where an evening file finds them: in process, with the next step named and dated. The Bureau of Labor Statistics put October consumer prices up 0.4 percent and core prices up 0.3 percent for a third straight month, a tenth above the consensus on both measures, in the Reuters account filed below; the print met the test Governor Waller had set that morning for considering a half-point increase in December. Wall Street closed lower—the S&P 500 down 0.38 percent at 7,520.93, the Nasdaq Composite down 0.74 percent at 25,065.88, the Dow down 0.30 percent at 52,231.89, Nvidia down 5.47 percent—and Brent settled at $91.49 after trading below ninety dollars for the first time since August. Secretary Hegseth, at his first Pentagon press conference since May, called the eight articles a farce, a stunt and sabotage; the House took up a procedural motion in the evening and no result was in the file at 1800. In Abu Dhabi the first day ended after about four hours with no agreement announced and a second day set for Wednesday. In Jerusalem the request to replace Speaker Ohana carried 67 signatures and the vote was set for November 17. Neither Senate race was called.

The Number, Whole: A Tenth Hot on Both Measures, and the Governor’s Test Met

The day’s one scheduled number is now a closed fact, and it corrects the consensus this paper printed at 0400. The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent in October after 0.6 percent in September; core prices rose 0.3 percent, as in September and in August. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 0.3 and 0.2. Inside the index, energy rose 0.7 percent against 5.2 percent in September, food rose 0.5 percent, and shelter rose 0.3 percent and accounted for more than 30 percent of the monthly increase; real average hourly earnings were unchanged, in the bureau’s figures as carried filed below. No annual rate was published, because the bureau collected no October 2025 data during last year’s lapse in appropriations. The next report, covering November, is scheduled for December 10, one day after the Federal Reserve meeting this report feeds.

The considered response came before the number, and the number met it. Governor Christopher Waller, speaking in London in remarks published at 0900 GMT, said he was leaning toward a 25-basis-point increase at the December 8–9 meeting even if October improved, and that if core prices rose around 0.3 percent or higher, a 50-basis-point increase should be considered, because hiking only 25 would put the Fed’s credibility at risk, in the London account and the market account of the speech filed below. Core printed 0.3 percent. The governor’s condition is met on his own stated terms; the committee’s decision has not been taken and is not his alone. The pricing accounts filed below put a December increase at 95.6 percent in one instrument and near 99 percent in another; they agree on the direction and differ on the figure, and both figures stand in the Cocked Hat.

Washington, Whole: Twenty-Five Minutes at the Pentagon, and a Vote Taken Up but Not Read Out

Secretary Hegseth answered the articles in public, by name, and without conceding any of them. In his first Pentagon press conference since May, he said no Secretary of War or Secretary of Defense has ever been impeached in 250 years for carrying out lawful military operations, and that the effort is about policy disagreements and not high crimes, in the Reuters account filed below. The other accounts carry the sharper words: a farce and a stunt, and “This is not patriotism. This is sabotage,” in the Washington account filed below. Vice President Vance, in a post before the vote, posed the question whether the secretary had committed impeachable crimes and answered, “obviously not,” in the live account filed below. House Democratic Leader Jeffries has said he will vote to impeach. The articles are unchanged since Monday: three charging the Iran campaign under the War Powers Resolution, and the rest covering the school strike at Minab, the vessel strikes, Venezuela, Yemen, and the alleged retaliation against Senator Kelly. They are allegations in a charging document, found by no court.

The evening’s business was the procedural motion, and at 1800 the file holds the motion, not its result. Representative Massie posted that the House votes today: first on a procedural motion to kill the resolution, such as a motion to refer it to committee, and, if that effort is overcome, on to debate and a vote on the articles, in the vote account and the procedure account filed below. The schedule put the first and last votes at 1730. One account filed before the vote says that if the motion to refer fails, the House would likely set a vote on the articles themselves for November 11, and that Mr. Massie would request separate votes on each article. A simple majority impeaches in the House; conviction requires two-thirds of the Senate. The prediction accounts filed below price impeachment by December 31 at 79 percent on two exchanges; a price is not a vote, and the desk prints it as a price. No tally, no outcome, and no statement from either leader after a vote is in the evening file, and the desk does not supply one. The log proceeds to the midnight watch for the result.

The Close: A Partial Retraction of Monday, Priced in Full

Wall Street’s reading of the day was given at the close, and it was a giving-back, not a rout. The S&P 500 closed down 0.38 percent at 7,520.93, the Nasdaq Composite down 0.74 percent at 25,065.88, the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 0.30 percent at 52,231.89, and the Russell 2000 down 0.68 percent, in the closing account and the closing table filed below; the indexes closed well above their session lows, having fallen as much as 1.7 percent on the Nasdaq in early afternoon. The ten-year Treasury yield finished at 4.983 percent, up 11.9 basis points, after touching 5.03 percent in the day. Nvidia closed down 5.47 percent at $168.89, the second straight fall, and the technology sector was the worst of the eleven sectors. Gold fell about 2 percent in the accounts filed below; the figures differ by instrument and hour and stand in the Cocked Hat. One closing summary filed below runs the day larger—the S&P 500 down 0.99 percent and the Nasdaq 100 down 1.50 percent—on a different index and a different hour; the desk prints the disagreement rather than averaging it.

Oil finished the sentence the morning began. Brent for January settlement declined 1.2 percent to settle at $91.49 a barrel, after falling as much as 3.7 percent in the day and trading below ninety dollars for the first time since late August, at $89.88 in one intraday account; West Texas Intermediate declined 0.9 percent to settle at $86.04, in the settlement account and the oil account filed below. The benchmark that settled at $92.57 on Monday is down about $30 since the midterm elections on the accounts’ tally, on the cause they have named throughout: a president holding off further strikes on Iran. Beside the close, the day’s second large document held: Anthropic’s amended filing offers 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78, raising up to $64.35 billion, with a separate $26 billion private placement beside it and trading expected on the Nasdaq under ANT near November 19, in the filing accounts filed below. The valuation figures differ by definition—$1.404 trillion fully diluted against about $968 billion at the midpoint on the filing’s post-offering share count—and stand as a difference of definition in the Cocked Hat.

Abu Dhabi, Whole: About Four Hours, the Subjects Named, and the Land Carried to Wednesday

The first day of the three-way talks is a closed day with an open result. The delegations concluded the first day on Tuesday after nearly four hours in the Associated Press account, and after four and a half hours including a break of about forty minutes in a second account, in the wire account and the duration account filed below; the desk prints both durations. The Russian delegation is led by Presidential Aide Vladimir Medinsky, the Ukrainian by Rustem Umerov, and the American by Messrs. Witkoff and Kushner. President Zelensky, briefed by his team, said the sides discussed humanitarian measures, prisoner-of-war releases, security guarantees and de-escalation, in the first-day account filed below. Secretary Rubio, speaking in Paris after the first day, described the talks as “very productive” and said, “Obviously, there is still a lot of work to be done. This is not something that can be resolved in the next 24 hours.” No agreement, joint statement, or separate statement followed the first day in the wire accounts. One partisan account filed below calls the day a collapse and reports President Zelensky rejecting any exchange of Donbas territory; no delegation’s public statement in the file confirms a collapse, and the desk prints the claim as that account’s claim, beside the wire record of a day adjourned to Wednesday morning, November 11. The fighting did not pause while the delegations talked, in the same account’s closing line, and no account in the file reports that it did.

Paris, Whole: Europe at the Table, and an Ask for Interceptors

The G7’s second day in Paris closed with the transatlantic sentence spoken by the American, and a material ask spoken by the guest. Secretary Rubio dismissed concerns of a rift over the Ukraine negotiations: “I don’t think there’s a difference. I think we have the same interest in mind,” and, “Europe’s at the table. They’re with us,” adding that Washington thinks the trilateral should eventually include the European partners, in the Paris account filed below. Germany’s sentence stands from the morning: Europe belongs at this table, and no fundamental change to Europe’s security architecture is necessary. The Kremlin’s stands against both: the negotiations remain trilateral. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said after talks with Secretary Rubio on the sidelines that he had urged Washington to accelerate interceptor deliveries as Russia targets the power grid ahead of winter, and that Ukraine remained prepared to discuss de-escalatory measures including ceasefires covering the Black Sea and energy infrastructure, with the Black Sea proposals conveyed through intermediaries including Turkey, Egypt and India, in the Reuters account filed below. France had indicated the meeting might produce no joint statement; none is in the evening file, and the desk files its absence as an absence.

Jerusalem, Whole: Sixty-Seven Signatures, a Date Set, and Two Speeches

Jerusalem supplied the day’s only dated decision. The 26th Knesset was sworn in on Tuesday. The opposition named Matan Kahana of Yashar as its candidate for speaker, to replace Amir Ohana of Likud, and Avigdor Liberman to head the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, in the candidate account filed below. In the fuller account filed below, the request to replace the speaker carried the signatures of 67 lawmakers—above the 61 required—and Speaker Ohana scheduled the vote for Tuesday, November 17, at 1600; the same account carries President Herzog’s plea that leaders “extend a hand to make concessions, even between rivals,” and the opening bills of Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc, for a state commission of inquiry into the October 7, 2023 attack, a limit on a prime minister’s time in office, and a repeal of the judicial overhaul, in the swearing-in account filed below. A second account records the two principals trading attacks at the ceremony—Prime Minister Netanyahu using the occasion against the government his rival is trying to form, and Mr. Eisenkot answering within the hour—in the ceremony account filed below. Mr. Ohana took the oath and holds the chair until the vote. Mr. Eisenkot’s mandate, given November 8, runs 28 days with a possible 14-day extension; Mr. Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister. One figure still disagrees with itself: 46 first-time members in Tuesday’s candidate account against 47 in the overnight file. Both stand in the Cocked Hat.

Krak&oacute;w, Whole: Thirteen in Hospital, a Computer Examined, and No Finding Stated

Krak&oacute;w’s Tuesday file is a hospital count and an instrument, not a conclusion. Thirteen of the fifteen injured remained in Krak&oacute;w hospitals on Tuesday, the regional governor said in the account filed below; one patient was discharged on Monday and an Austrian patient was transferred to Austria. The autopsies of the nine victims, begun Monday and expected to take about two days, had produced no published findings by collection time. Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek told Radio Krak&oacute;w on Tuesday that investigators had accessed the gunman’s computer and found evidence of visits to websites about Anders Breivik, in the Tuesday account filed below. The minister’s statement is a statement about a computer; it is not a finding of motive. The prosecutors’ standing limit stands beside it: they have no findings that would let them state responsibly that the gunman was inspired by any particular ideology. Both sentences are in the file, and the desk prints both, in the mourning account filed below and in the Tuesday account. The city’s mourning runs through tomorrow, November 11. The wounded counts that have disagreed since Saturday—15 in the governor’s hospital count, 16 and 17 in earlier printings that include the gunman or the first day’s tally—stand in the Cocked Hat, unresolved.

Iran, Whole: No New Sentence, and a Settlement as the Market’s Translation

Neither capital added a sentence to the Iran file on Tuesday, and the file at evening is Monday’s, with one price changed underneath it. The president’s position stands: fresh strikes held off for now after appeals from Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the Emirates, Bahrain and Kuwait; the naval blockade kept in place; the war described by the president on Monday as militarily “effectively over” and his forces as locked and loaded, in the pause account and the effectively-over account filed below. Tehran’s two registers stand: negotiate with dignity, from its president; imaginary talks and the seven conditions, from its security council secretary. Secretary Rubio’s sentence stands against both: no progress, and the demands not realistic. The one unconfirmed enrichment report in the morning file remains unconfirmed by either government at evening. Brent’s settlement at $91.49, after a trade below ninety, is the day’s movement in this file, and it is financial, not verbal. What the two capitals agree on remains what they agreed on at midnight: the blockade exists. It is imposed in one account and demanded lifted in the other, and it stood all day.

The Count, Whole: Mississippi’s Deadline Day Ends, Alaska’s Batch Still Out

For a seventh day neither Senate race was called, and Tuesday moved both files by deadline and by one afternoon figure, not by a call. In Mississippi, Tuesday was the last day for mail ballots postmarked by Election Day to arrive and for affidavit voters to cure their identification. The afternoon tally in the account filed below, as of 1455 ET, put Mr. Colom ahead by about 2,700 votes, at 49.1 percent to 48.8 percent with 99 percent counted in that account’s tally, in the clarity account filed below; the Associated Press estimate carried in this paper stands at about 97 percent counted and a margin of 2,574 in its last raw posting, and the two completeness figures stand unreconciled in the Cocked Hat. About 3,600 mail ballots were outstanding under the secretary of state’s November 4 statement. Counties certify by November 13, and Mississippi has no automatic recount provision. In Alaska, Monday’s count stands as the last posted count at evening: Ms. Peltola 106,321 to Mr. Sullivan 103,804, a margin of 2,517 first-choice votes, up from 637, in the widening account and the Juneau account filed below. The Tuesday batch—tens of thousands of early, absentee and questioned ballots, expected in the state’s afternoon, which is Washington’s night—had not posted in the file at 1800 ET, and one account expects it Tuesday night. The senator and the president have questioned the count on the ground that a second candidate named Daniel Sullivan drew 3,651 votes, more than the margin; the challenger’s campaign answers that the count is the system working as designed. No candidate is near 50 percent of first choices, and the ranked-choice tabulation is set for November 18, with certification targeted for November 25. Sixteen congressional races in all remain uncalled in the account filed below, fourteen of them in the House. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide, and Colorado’s 4th District stands uncalled with them.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On Abu Dhabi’s duration, nearly four hours in the wire account against four and a half including a break in a second. On Abu Dhabi’s character, a productive first day in the secretary’s word and an adjournment without agreement in the wire record, against a collapse in one partisan account that no delegation’s statement confirms. On the December increase, 95.6 percent in one pricing instrument, near 99 percent in another, and better than 80 percent before the print in a third—three instruments, one direction. On the close, one summary’s S&P 500 down 0.99 percent on a later hour and a different measure, against the closing table’s 0.38 percent. On gold, down 1.82 percent in futures in one account and 2.7 percent in an exchange-traded print in another. On Anthropic, $1.404 trillion fully diluted against about $968 billion at the midpoint on the post-offering count: a difference of definition. On Jerusalem’s new members, 46 against 47. On Mississippi’s completeness, 99 percent in the afternoon tally against about 97 percent in the wire estimate. On Krak&oacute;w’s wounded, 15, 16 and 17 across the week’s printings. On the Hegseth vote, a schedule, two leaders’ stated intentions, and a 79 percent market price—and no tally in the file. Against the triangle, the evening’s single-valued facts are these: prices rose 0.4 percent and core prices 0.3 percent in October, a tenth hot on both measures; Governor Waller’s stated condition was met by the core print; Wall Street closed lower on all four indexes and Brent settled at $91.49 after trading below ninety; Secretary Hegseth spoke and conceded nothing; Abu Dhabi’s first day ended without an announced agreement and resumes Wednesday; 67 lawmakers signed to replace Speaker Ohana and the vote is set for November 17; thirteen of Krak&oacute;w’s injured remain in hospital; and no Senate race and no impeachment article was decided in the file by 1800. The log proceeds to the midnight watch.

 The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 36 items.

 

 SubjectiveReuters, via SRN News — a hot October inflation report rattles marketsUnited States consumer prices increased more than expected in October, leaving the Federal Reserve on course to raise interest rates next month. The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent after advancing 0.6 percent in September; economists polled by Reuters had forecast 0.3 percent. Core prices rose 0.3 percent, against a forecast of 0.2 percent. Year-over-year readings were not published because last year’s shutdown prevented collection of October 2025 data; annual inflation was 3.7 percent in September.

 SubjectiveThe Hindu BusinessLine — consumer inflation slows to 0.4 percent in October as energy pressures easeThe Consumer Price Index increased 0.4 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in October after rising 0.6 percent in September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Core inflation was unchanged at 0.3 percent, the same rate as September and August. Energy prices increased 0.7 percent, sharply slower than September’s 5.2 percent rise; food prices rose 0.5 percent. No annual rate was published, because comparable October 2025 data were unavailable following the lapse in appropriations.

 SubjectiveThe Hindu BusinessLine, carrying Reuters — Governor Waller plans to support at least a quarter-point rate hike in DecemberFederal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday he would support raising short-term borrowing costs next month even if the data showed inflation cooled, and would consider an upsized half-point increase if the picture worsened. If core consumer prices rise 0.3 percent or more from September, a 50-basis-point hike should be considered at the December meeting, he said, adding that hiking only 25 would put the Fed’s credibility at risk.

 SubjectiveBigGo Finance — Governor Waller signals a December rate hike, 50 basis points if neededGovernor Waller said publicly on November 10 in London that he supports a December rate hike and drew a data threshold for its size: if the October core CPI gain remained around 0.3 percent or higher, he would support a 50-basis-point increase. Markets reacted swiftly: Nasdaq 100 futures fell, spot gold’s intraday decline widened to about 1 percent, and the dollar strengthened. The account carries CME FedWatch at 95.6 percent for a 25-basis-point December increase.

 SubjectiveInvestopedia — stocks fall, Treasury yields jump as rate-hike concerns mount after the hot inflation reportStocks closed lower Tuesday, though well above their session lows, following an inflation report that reinforced expectations the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates again soon. The Nasdaq Composite shed 0.7 percent after falling as much as 1.7 percent in early-afternoon trading, while the Dow and the S&P 500 finished down 0.3 and 0.4 percent. The ten-year Treasury yield was at 4.98 percent, down from an intraday high of 5.03 percent. Nvidia dropped 5.5 percent to pace Dow decliners.

The ten-year yield finished at 4.983 percent, up 11.9 basis points.

 SubjectiveMarketOne — the closing bell, November 10, 2026Stocks slid across the board as a hotter-than-expected inflation print collided with a hawkish Fed and sent chip stocks and growth names into retreat. The S&P 500 fell 0.5 percent, the Nasdaq-heavy QQQ dropped 0.9 percent, and small caps gave back 0.8 percent.  SubjectiveXTB — daily summary: the CPI reading hits marketsHigher-than-forecast United States inflation—core CPI plus 0.3 percent on the month, headline plus 0.4 percent—sparked a hawkish reaction from Fed officials, and Wall Street came under strong selling pressure following the release. The summary’s figures, at its 2047 print: the S&P 500 falls 0.99 percent, the Nasdaq 100 falls 1.50 percent, and the Dow Jones falls 0.70 percent.

 SubjectiveRigzone, carrying Bloomberg — oil prices retreat as peace hopes growBrent crude fell, briefly slumping below $90 a barrel, as technical factors helped deepen a selloff driven by expectations of further de-escalation in the Iran war. The global benchmark settled below $92 after declining as much as 3.7 percent on Tuesday: Brent for January settlement declined 1.2 percent to settle at $91.49 a barrel, and West Texas Intermediate for December delivery declined 0.9 percent to settle at $86.04 a barrel in New York.

 SubjectiveOilPrice.com — oil falls to its lowest level since AugustBrent crude briefly fell below $90 a barrel as hopes of diplomatic breakthroughs in Iran and Ukraine accelerated the oil market selloff. Crude prices have plunged by almost $30 a barrel since the United States midterm elections. The administration reiterated its reluctance to engage in new military strikes against Iran.

 SubjectiveTechCrunch — Anthropic sets an IPO price range of $70 to $78 a shareAnthropic, in an updated prospectus filed Tuesday, will offer 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78 a share, reaching an implied valuation of $1.404 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The offering would raise $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion. Trading is expected on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT.

 SubjectiveTronWeekly — Anthropic’s offering: $64.4 billion, 825 million shares at $70 to $78Anthropic offered 825 million Class A shares at $70.00 to $78.00 apiece in its initial public offering on November 10, 2026: 801,351,354 shares offered by the company and 23,648,646 by shareholders, with an underwriters’ option for up to 123,750,000 more. ### Inflation Runs Hot at 0.4 Percent, Hegseth Calls the Charges a Farce, and Abu Dhabi\u2019s First Day Ends Without a Breakthrough

Filed as: Edition No. 29 — The Midday Watch · 2026-11-10T12:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-10-midday-watch.html

The Midday File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Inflation Runs Hot at 0.4 Percent, Hegseth Calls the Charges a Farce, and Abu Dhabi’s First Day Ends Without a Breakthrough

 The news at midday: the morning’s one scheduled number came in a tenth hotter than the morning expected it, on both measures; the morning’s one scheduled witness answered his accusers for twenty-five minutes and the vote on him moved up a day; the market that rose on Monday gave back part of the rise at the open and then steadied on a filing; and the two tables the week opened—Abu Dhabi and Paris—produced a duration, a seating plan and no agreement by noon.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Tuesday, November 10, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 28, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today, and from Edition No. 27, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today. Where the midday figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open, and the earlier editions stand unrevised, as a log stands.

The Midday in Brief

Midday corrected the morning on the number, on the vote, and on the speaker, and it left every negotiation and every count exactly where the night left them. The Bureau of Labor Statistics put October’s consumer prices up 0.4 percent on the month and core prices up 0.3 percent, in the Reuters account filed below; the overnight edition carried a consensus of 0.3 and 0.2, and the correction is a tenth on each measure, stated in the section below. At the Pentagon, Secretary Hegseth held his first press conference since May and called Representative Massie’s eight articles a farce, a stunt and sabotage, in the Washington account filed below; Mr. Massie answered that the House votes today, on a procedural motion first, with votes expected at 1730—not Wednesday, as the midnight file had it. In New York the three main indexes opened lower, the ten-year yield stood near 4.99 percent, and Brent crude traded below ninety dollars for the first time since August, before the Anthropic filing, printed below, steadied the technology shares by mid-morning. In Abu Dhabi the first day of the three-way talks ended after nearly four hours and resumes Wednesday, with no breakthrough announced. In Jerusalem the opposition named its candidate for speaker, Matan Kahana of Yashar, and the 26th Knesset opened in the afternoon with Speaker Ohana taking the oath and the chair. Neither Senate race was called by noon, and no new figure for either was published in the morning.

The Correction at Noon: The Number Came In a Tenth Hot on Both Measures

The day’s first official statement was a number, and the number corrects the consensus this paper printed at 0400. The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers rose 0.4 percent in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, after rising 0.6 percent in September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said in its release; core prices, excluding food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, as they did in September and in August—a third straight month at that rate, in the bureau’s figures as carried and the release account filed below. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 0.3 percent on the headline and 0.2 percent on the core. The overnight edition carried that consensus; the print is a tenth above it on both measures, and the desk files the correction at the head of the edition, where corrections belong. Inside the index: energy rose 0.7 percent, against 5.2 percent in September, with gasoline up 1.0 percent against 9.1 percent; food rose 0.5 percent, with food at home up 0.4 percent; shelter rose 0.3 percent and accounted for more than 30 percent of the monthly increase; real average hourly earnings were unchanged on the month. No annual rate was published, for the reason the overnight edition gave: the bureau collected no October 2025 data during last year’s lapse in appropriations, so there is no October-to-October comparison to print. September’s annual rate, 3.7 percent, remains a September figure. The next report, covering November, is scheduled for December 10—one day after the Federal Reserve meeting this report now feeds.

The print met, exactly, the test a governor of the Federal Reserve had set for it four and a half hours before it landed. Governor Christopher Waller, speaking in London in remarks published at 0900 GMT, said he was leaning toward supporting a 25-basis-point increase at the December 8–9 meeting even if October improved on September, and that if core prices rose around 0.3 percent or higher, a 50-basis-point increase should be considered, because hiking only 25 would put the Fed’s credibility at risk, in the London account and the remarks account filed below. Core printed 0.3 percent. The governor’s condition is therefore met on his own stated terms; the committee’s decision is not his alone and has not been taken. The market’s pricing moved in the same direction before and after the release: traders priced an almost 99 percent chance of a December increase in one account filed below, fully priced two quarter-point increases by March in another, and had priced better than 80 percent for December before the print. The accounts differ on the instrument and the hour; they agree on the direction, and the desk prints the agreement and the differing figures in the Cocked Hat.

Washington at Noon: Twenty-Five Minutes at the Pentagon, a Vote at 1730

Secretary Hegseth answered the articles the way the articles were filed—in public, by name, and without conceding any of them. In his first Pentagon press conference since May—six months in the Associated Press count, 180 days in the count this paper has carried—the secretary said no Secretary of War or Secretary of Defense has ever been impeached in 250 years for carrying out lawful military operations, that the effort is about policy disagreements and not high crimes, and that his accuser is a rogue lawmaker, in the Associated Press account filed below. The other accounts carry the same sentences in his sharper words: a farce and a stunt, in the Reuters account; “This is not patriotism. This is sabotage,” in the briefing account; and, on the troops, that anyone coming for the warriors would have to come through him, in the Pentagon account filed below. On the record he defends, he cited Operation Epic Fury’s more than 13,000 targets struck and the destruction of Iran’s navy and of more than 80 percent of its nuclear industrial base; those are the secretary’s figures, printed as his. The conference lasted roughly 25 minutes and took a handful of questions. The articles themselves are unchanged since Monday: three charging the Iran campaign under the War Powers Resolution, and the rest covering the school strike at Minab, the vessel strikes, Venezuela, Yemen, and the alleged retaliation against Senator Kelly. They are allegations in a charging document, found by no court.

The second correction of the day is the House’s clock. The midnight edition carried House leaders as having until Wednesday to table, refer or vote. On Tuesday morning Representative Massie posted that the House votes today: the first vote is on a procedural motion to kill the resolution, such as a motion to refer it to committee, and if that effort is overcome the House proceeds to debate and a vote on the articles, in the schedule account and the Reuters account filed below. The daily schedule Mr. Massie shared puts the House in at 1000 for morning hour and at noon for legislative business, with the first and last votes expected at 1730. At noon the procedural motion stands listed and unvoted. A simple majority impeaches in the House; conviction and removal would require two-thirds of the Senate, where Republicans hold 53 seats in the accounts filed below. Whatever Tuesday evening decides, the accounts agree the effort returns in January if it fails now, when the new Congress is sworn in on January 3.

The Markets’ Reading at Noon: A Hotter Print, a Lower Open, and Oil Below Ninety

Wall Street’s reading of the morning was given at the open, and it was a partial retraction of Monday, not a reversal of it. The Dow fell 226.5 points, or 0.43 percent, at the open to 52,163.21; the S&P 500 fell 36.8 points, or 0.49 percent, to 7,513.09; and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 205.7 points, or 0.81 percent, to 25,047.448, in the Reuters snapshot filed below. A second snapshot at 0948 ran a touch lower on all three—the Dow down 0.47 percent, the S&P 500 down 0.58 percent, the Nasdaq down 0.70 percent—with the ten-year Treasury yield at 4.988 percent, up from Monday’s close of 4.862 percent, in the early-session account filed below. Nvidia fell 2.6 percent in one opening account and 1.6 percent in a pre-open account; the chip shares that led Monday’s rise gave back part of it. Europe, which had risen into the number—the FTSE 100 up 0.5 percent at London’s midday, the CAC 40 up 1.2 percent and the DAX up 1.3 percent, in the London midday account filed below—pared its gains after it. Oil completed the morning’s sentence: Brent fell more than 3 percent and traded below ninety dollars a barrel for the first time since late August, at $89.88 in one account, with West Texas Intermediate down more than 2 percent to below $85, in the global markets account filed below. The same barrel that settled at $92.57 on Monday has now fallen through two round numbers in two days, on the same cause the accounts have named throughout: a president holding off further strikes on Iran.

By mid-morning the fall had steadied, and the steadying had a name. Both Nasdaq indexes erased their opening losses and traded into positive territory as attention shifted to Anthropic’s planned listing, before backing off to stand near unchanged, in the rebound account filed below. The filing behind the move is the morning’s second large document. Anthropic, in an updated prospectus filed Tuesday, will offer 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78 a share, raising $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion, at a valuation of up to $1.404 trillion on a fully diluted basis, in the filing account filed below; the Reuters accounts put the non-diluted value at about $1 trillion to $1.02 trillion, the difference being the treatment of options and restricted stock, in the Reuters account and the exclusive account filed below. A separate $26 billion private placement with cornerstone investors including Google, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices stands beside the offering. The terms filed Tuesday are lower than the terms briefly circulated to bankers on Monday night and retracted—about 867 million shares at up to $80—and lower than the $2 trillion discussed earlier in the year, against a May private valuation of $965 billion. Run-rate revenue stood at $81 billion at the end of October. Trading is expected on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT near November 19. On the morning the print argued for dearer money, the largest test of the AI boom priced itself anyway, at a lower price than it first asked.

Abu Dhabi at Noon: Four Hours, a Framework Proposed, and the Land Left for Wednesday

The talks the overnight edition filed as open are, at noon, adjourned for the day, and the day produced a duration and a method and no result. The first day concluded after nearly four hours, the RIA Novosti account said, and the talks are expected to resume Wednesday, according to the press office of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, in the Associated Press account filed below. The day’s order is on the record: it began with a meeting of the Ukrainian team, the American envoys and representatives of the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission, and then moved to the trilateral format with Russia. Mr. Kushner, opening, said the United States wanted to draw lessons from previous efforts and develop a new structure, and Washington is pressing a new European security framework, in the framework account filed below. One account citing an American official puts day one on policing a future ceasefire, with territory waiting until day two, and reports the same official saying both sides had privately shown some flexibility over a possible swap of territory, in the running-order account filed below. That flexibility rests on one unnamed official’s briefing and is printed as such. The stated positions have not moved in public, and no breakthrough has been announced by any delegation. The desk files four hours, a framework proposed, and the land question carried to Wednesday.

Paris at Noon: The Second Day, Ukraine’s Minister in the Room, No Statement in the File

The G7’s two days in Paris ran out at midday with the argument it opened with, now spoken by the guest as well as the hosts. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, joined Tuesday’s session on Ukraine—air defence, economic pressure, Black Sea navigation—having said before departing, “No one has the right to decide our fate behind our backs,” in the Paris account filed below. Germany’s sentence stands: Europe belongs at this table, and no fundamental change to Europe’s security architecture is necessary, right or appropriate—an answer, in substance, to the framework Mr. Kushner proposed in Abu Dhabi the same morning. France’s stands: Europeans will participate in the Abu Dhabi discussions. The Kremlin’s stands against both: the negotiations remain trilateral. The Abu Dhabi lists at noon agree with the Kremlin on the main table and with France on the rooms around it. The second session took up instability in the Middle East, with the European ministers warning against renewed American strikes on Iran and arguing for restoring normal shipping through Hormuz, in the ministers account filed below. Canada announced fresh sanctions on Russia on Monday. France had indicated the meeting might produce no joint statement; at noon none is in the file, and the desk files its absence as an absence, not as a rupture.

Jerusalem at Noon: A Candidate Named, an Oath Taken, and the Chair Held for Now

Jerusalem supplied the day’s third correction: the unnamed speaker of the overnight file has a name. The opposition bloc on Tuesday chose former minister Matan Kahana of Mr. Eisenkot’s Yashar party as its candidate for speaker, to replace Amir Ohana of Likud, in the candidate account filed below. The naming settles the question the mandate carried from Sunday—who, if the chair changes hands—and leaves the other two open: at least 61 members must sign or vote for a replacement, Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc stands at 48, and Mr. Ohana has said he will not hold the vote on inauguration day but will schedule it within the following week on a valid request. The ceremony itself ran on its printed schedule: a plaza ceremony at 1520 Jerusalem time and the plenary at 1600, which is 0900 in Washington. In the opening broadcast account, President Herzog addressed the session, called on lawmakers to debate with respect, and invited Speaker Ohana to take the oath before handing him the chair; Mr. Ohana pledged, Psalm 122 was recited, and the roll-call pledges of the 120 members proceeded under his chairmanship, with one warning issued to a member over an interruption, in the opening account filed below. The account itself cautions that the broadcast segments reviewed do not establish that all 120 oaths were completed, and the desk prints the caution with the fact. Mr. Ohana’s assumption of the chair for the opening is a step in the ceremony, not the outcome of the speaker question; Mr. Netanyahu remains prime minister, and the mandate runs to December 6. One figure in the file disagrees with itself: the overnight edition carried 47 first-time members, and Tuesday’s candidate account carries 46. The desk prints both in the Cocked Hat and settles neither.

Iran at Noon: No New Sentence, and a Barrel Below Ninety as the Market’s Translation

Neither capital added a sentence to the Iran file in the morning, and the file at noon is the standing one, with one price changed underneath it. The president’s position stands as Monday’s: fresh strikes held off for now after appeals from Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the Emirates, Bahrain and Kuwait; the naval blockade and Operation Iron Gate kept in place; forces locked and loaded if the position changes, in the Reuters account and the pause account filed below. Tehran’s two registers stand: negotiate with dignity, from its president; imaginary talks and the seven conditions, from its security council secretary. Secretary Rubio’s sentence stands against both: no progress, and the demands not realistic. One unconfirmed report in the morning file says, on unnamed sources, that the United States is prepared to let Iran keep enriching uranium at 3.67 percent and that Tehran is willing to accept that limit; neither government has confirmed it, and the desk files it as one unconfirmed report, not as a term. The movement in the file is financial, not verbal: Brent’s fall below ninety dollars is the market’s translation of the pause. What the two capitals agree on remains what they agreed on at midnight: the blockade exists. It is imposed in one account and demanded lifted in the other, and it stood all morning.

Krak&oacute;w at Noon: The Autopsies’ Second Day, and No Findings Published

Krak&oacute;w’s file at noon is an instrument running, not a result. The autopsies of the nine victims, begun Monday, were expected to take about two days, which puts their completion at about today; no findings from them had been published by noon, and the desk does not fill the space where findings will go. The standing facts are Monday’s: the suspect died at about 0430 on Monday after at least three operations; the case against the dead man will in time be closed while the investigation around him—whether he acted alone or was inspired, the phones, computers and 11 firearms under analysis—continues; and the prosecutors’ limit stands, that they have no findings that would let them state responsibly that he was inspired by any particular ideology. The interior ministry’s review of gun licensing, announced after police data showed more than 50,000 new licences issued in 2025, is the file’s one new policy instrument; both the gunman and his father held permits. The city’s own mourning runs through tomorrow, November 11. The wounded stand at 15 in hospital in the governor’s count, against 17 in the prosecutors’ earlier count; the disagreement is carried in the Cocked Hat, as it has been since Monday.

The Count at Noon: Both Deadlines Fall Today, and No New Figure by Noon

For a sixth day neither Senate race was called, and the morning published no new figure for either race; Tuesday’s part in both files is deadlines, not numbers, until the counts run. Alaska’s next scheduled count falls today, carrying early votes cast October 30 to November 2, absentee and questioned ballots, on a race standing in the last state posting at Mary Peltola 102,962 to Dan Sullivan 102,325—a margin of 637 first-choice votes, with no candidate near 50 percent and the ranked-choice tabulation set for November 18. A running results account updated Tuesday carries the same race in rounder figures as of November 9—Ms. Peltola at 48.6 percent to Mr. Sullivan’s 47.5 percent, more than 220,000 ballots counted and about 78.5 percent of ballots in, in the running account filed below; the percentages and the raw posting are two printings of one standing count, not two counts. Mississippi’s deadlines fall today: mail ballots postmarked by Election Day must arrive and affidavit voters must cure their identification, on a race standing at Scott Colom 467,930 to Cindy Hyde-Smith 465,356, a margin of 2,574 on about 97 percent counted in the Associated Press estimate; the same running account carries Mississippi in percentages as 49.1 to 48.8 with 99 percent counted, a figure the desk cannot reconcile with the 97 percent estimate and prints as a disagreement in the Cocked Hat, in the delay account filed below. Counties certify by November 13, and Mississippi has no automatic recount provision. Alaska’s count, when it posts, will move in the state’s afternoon, which is Washington’s evening; the midday file therefore closes the count where the night left it, with both of its named days arrived and neither of its numbers yet moved. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide. Colorado’s 4th District stands uncalled with them.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On the December increase, almost 99 percent in one pricing account, fully priced by March in another, and better than 80 percent before the print in a third—three instruments, one direction. On Anthropic, $1.404 trillion fully diluted against about $1.02 trillion not diluted: a difference of definition, printed as one. On the open, the Reuters snapshot and the 0948 snapshot differing by tenths on all three indexes, as snapshots an hour apart will. On Abu Dhabi’s flexibility, one unnamed official’s briefing against every delegation’s public silence. On the enrichment report, one unconfirmed account against no confirmation from either capital. On Jerusalem’s new members, 47 in the overnight file and 46 in Tuesday’s candidate account. On Mississippi’s completeness, about 97 percent in the wire estimate and 99 percent in the running account, irreconcilable at noon. On Krak&oacute;w’s wounded, 15 in the governor’s hospital count against 17 in the prosecutors’ earlier count. Against the triangle, the midday’s single-valued facts are these: prices rose 0.4 percent and core prices 0.3 percent in October, a tenth hot on both measures against the consensus, with no annual rate in existence; Governor Waller’s stated condition for considering a half-point increase was met by the core print; Secretary Hegseth spoke for about 25 minutes and conceded nothing; the House’s first vote on his articles is set for Tuesday evening; Brent traded below ninety dollars; Anthropic filed at $70 to $78; Abu Dhabi’s first day ran nearly four hours and produced no announced breakthrough; Matan Kahana is the opposition’s candidate for speaker and Amir Ohana holds the chair; and no Senate race was called. The log proceeds to the evening.

 The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 35 items.

 

 SubjectiveReuters, via SRN News — a hot October inflation report rattles marketsUnited States consumer prices increased more than expected in October, leaving the Federal Reserve on course to raise interest rates next month. The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent last month after advancing 0.6 percent in September; economists polled by Reuters had forecast 0.3 percent. Core prices rose 0.3 percent, against a forecast of 0.2 percent. The bureau did not publish year-over-year readings because last year’s shutdown prevented collection of October 2025 data; annual inflation was 3.7 percent in September. Governor Waller, the account notes, had said the central bank ought to raise borrowing costs in December even if inflation cooled.

 SubjectiveThe Hindu BusinessLine — consumer inflation slows to 0.4 percent in October as energy pressures easeThe Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers increased 0.4 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in October after rising 0.6 percent in September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Core inflation was unchanged at 0.3 percent, the same rate as September and August. Energy prices increased 0.7 percent, sharply slower than September’s 5.2 percent rise; food prices rose 0.5 percent after remaining unchanged in September. No annual rate was published, because comparable October 2025 data were unavailable following the lapse in appropriations.

Core inflation rose 0.3 percent. The report is the last look at consumer prices the Federal Reserve will get before its December meeting, and one economist quoted says it most likely seals a rate increase to close the year. The account carries the gasoline figures: regular gasoline up 34 percent and diesel up 64 percent since February 28, on AAA data, with the national average at $3.98 on November 10.

 SubjectiveSHRM — inflation continued to rise in OctoberThe consumer price index increased 0.4 percent in October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on November 10, higher than the 0.3 percent economists expected. Shelter rose 0.3 percent and accounted for more than 30 percent of the monthly increase; food increased 0.5 percent, with food at home up 0.4 percent and food away from home up 0.5 percent; energy increased 0.7 percent after jumping 5.2 percent in September. Real average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October.

 SubjectiveThe Hindu BusinessLine, carrying Reuters — Governor Waller plans to support at least a quarter-point rate hike in DecemberFederal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday he would support raising short-term borrowing costs next month even if the data showed inflation cooled, and would consider an upsized half-point increase if the picture worsened. If core consumer prices rise 0.3 percent or more from September, a 50-basis-point hike should be considered at the December meeting, he said, adding that hiking only 25 would put the Fed’s credibility at risk. Markets, the account says, had priced in about an 85 percent chance of a December increase to a 4.00 to 4.25 percent range.

 Subjectivepolitical.org — why the Mississippi and Alaska Senate races remain uncalled days after Election DayNearly a week after the November 3 midterms, the Senate contests in Mississippi and Alaska are the only two in the country that remain uncalled. In Mississippi, Mr. Colom led by 43 votes early on November 4 and was ahead by about 2,500 votes with 97 percent counted as of November 7; the deadline for counting ballots is Tuesday, November 10, and certification is Friday, November 13. In Alaska, Ms. Peltola leads by 637 votes with roughly a quarter of ballots outstanding; the ranked-choice tabulation is not expected until after the November 18 deadline for late absentee ballots. Mississippi has no automatic recount provision; Alaska’s contest carries a Justice Department lawsuit, rejected by a federal judge, and a public-records suit from the Peltola campaign, the account notes.
